items.prompt: What is the typical width of an oceanic trench?

options.label: A few meters
options.feedback: Trenches are far broader than that. Typical widths are 50 to 100 kilometers, making them substantial depressions on the ocean floor.

options.label: 1 to 2 kilometers
options.feedback: That is too narrow. Oceanic trenches usually span 50 to 100 kilometers across, not just one or two.

options.label: 50 to 100 kilometers
options.feedback: Correct. Oceanic trenches are 50 to 100 kilometers wide, though they can stretch for thousands of kilometers in length.

options.label: 500 to 1,000 kilometers
options.feedback: That is too wide. Trenches are typically 50 to 100 kilometers across, not hundreds of kilometers.

items.ok_line: Oceanic trenches are 50 to 100 kilometers wide.
items.ko_line: Typical trench width is 50 to 100 kilometers.
items.exp_text: Oceanic trenches are long, narrow depressions on the ocean floor. They are 50 to 100 kilometers wide but can be thousands of kilometers long, making them the largest linear depressions on Earth.

items.prompt: Where are most of the world's oceanic trenches located?

options.label: Around the Pacific Ocean
options.feedback: Correct. Most trenches are found around the Pacific Ocean, with some in the eastern Indian Ocean and a few elsewhere.

options.label: In the Atlantic Ocean
options.feedback: The Atlantic has few convergent margins, so most trenches are not there. The Pacific holds the majority.

options.label: In the Arctic Ocean
options.feedback: The Arctic is not a major location for trenches. They are concentrated in the Pacific and parts of the Indian Ocean.

options.label: In the Mediterranean Sea
options.feedback: The Mediterranean has only short convergent margin segments, not most of the world's trenches. The Pacific is the main region.

items.ok_line: Most trenches ring the Pacific Ocean.
items.ko_line: The Pacific hosts the majority of trenches.
items.exp_text: There are about 50,000 kilometers of oceanic trenches worldwide. Most are around the Pacific Ocean, but they also occur in the eastern Indian Ocean and a few other locations.

items.prompt: What shape is the profile of a typical oceanic trench?

options.label: U-shaped with a flat bottom
options.feedback: That describes a trough, not a trench. Trenches have a V-shaped profile, while troughs have steep sides and flat bottoms.

options.label: W-shaped with multiple ridges
options.feedback: Trenches do not have a W shape. They are single, V-shaped depressions with one lowest point.

options.label: Flat and wide
options.feedback: A flat profile would be a trough or basin. Trenches are narrow and V-shaped, not flat.

options.label: V-shaped
options.feedback: Correct. Oceanic trenches have an asymmetric V-shape, with one side steeper than the other.

items.ko_line: Troughs are flat-bottomed, trenches are V-shaped.
items.exp_text: An oceanic trench is an elongated depression with a V-shaped profile. This distinguishes it from a trough, which has steep sides and a flat bottom.

items.prompt: What marks the position of an oceanic trench?

options.label: The middle of a mid-ocean ridge
options.feedback: Mid-ocean ridges are where plates pull apart, not where they converge. Trenches are at convergent boundaries.

options.label: The point where one plate begins to descend beneath another
options.feedback: Correct. A trench marks where the subducting slab starts to plunge beneath another lithospheric slab.

options.label: The edge of a continental shelf
options.feedback: Continental shelves are shallow underwater extensions of continents. Trenches are far from these, at plate boundaries.

options.label: The center of an ocean basin
options.feedback: Ocean basin centers are not necessarily trenches. Trenches sit at the boundary where plates move toward each other.

items.ok_line: A trench is where subduction begins.
items.ko_line: Trenches mark the start of subduction.
items.exp_text: An oceanic trench marks the position at which the flexed, subducting slab begins to descend beneath another lithospheric slab. This happens at convergent plate boundaries.

items.prompt: What is the depth of the deepest point in the ocean, located in the Mariana Trench?

options.label: About 3,000 meters
options.feedback: That is too shallow. The deepest point is nearly 11,000 meters below sea level, far deeper than 3,000 meters.

options.label: About 7,000 meters
options.feedback: That is close but still too shallow. The Challenger Deep reaches about 10,994 meters.

options.label: About 10,994 meters
options.feedback: Correct. The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is about 10,994 meters below sea level, the greatest ocean depth.

options.label: About 15,000 meters
options.feedback: That is too deep. The deepest measured point is about 10,994 meters, not 15,000.

items.ok_line: Challenger Deep is about 10,994 meters deep.
items.ko_line: The deepest point is near 11 kilometers.
items.exp_text: The greatest ocean depth measured is in the Challenger Deep of the Mariana Trench, at about 10,994 meters below sea level. This is the lowest point on Earth's seafloor.

items.prompt: What is the slope angle of the steeper side of an oceanic trench?

options.label: 8 to 20 degrees
options.feedback: Correct. The inner (overriding) side of a trench has a steeper slope of 8 to 20 degrees.

options.label: About 5 degrees
options.feedback: That is the gentler slope found on the outer (subducting) side. The inner slope is steeper.

options.label: Less than 1 degree
options.feedback: That is too gentle for a trench. The steeper side typically ranges from 8 to 20 degrees.

options.label: 30 to 45 degrees
options.feedback: That is too steep. Trench slopes are not that extreme; the steepest side is 8 to 20 degrees.

items.ok_line: The steeper side is 8 to 20 degrees.
items.ko_line: About 5 degrees is the gentler outer side.
items.exp_text: Oceanic trenches have an asymmetric V-shape: the inner (overriding) side is steeper, 8 to 20 degrees, while the outer (subducting) side is gentler, around 5 degrees.

items.prompt: What feature forms on the ocean floor just before the outer slope of a trench?

options.label: A mid-ocean ridge
options.feedback: Mid-ocean ridges are spreading centers, not features of trenches. Before the outer slope, a subtle high forms.

options.label: A volcanic island arc
options.feedback: Island arcs are on the inner side, about 200 km from the trench, not on the outer slope.

options.label: A flat abyssal plain
options.feedback: Abyssal plains are wide flat areas, but near a trench the plate bends upward, creating a high.

options.label: An outer trench high
options.feedback: Correct. As the subducting plate bends upward before plunging, it creates a subtle outer trench high.

items.ok_line: A subtle high exists before the outer slope.
items.ko_line: The bend-up forms a low high.
items.exp_text: As the subducting plate approaches a trench, it bends slightly upward, creating an outer trench high. This is subtle, often tens of meters high, and located a few tens of kilometers from the trench axis.

items.prompt: What kind of organisms support unique biomes found at oceanic trenches?

options.label: Photosynthetic plants
options.feedback: Photosynthesis needs sunlight, which does not reach trench depths. These biomes rely on chemotrophic microorganisms.

options.label: Chemotrophic microorganisms
options.feedback: Correct. Unique biomes at trenches are based on chemotrophic microorganisms, which use chemical energy rather than sunlight.

options.label: Coral polyps
options.feedback: Corals need warm, shallow, sunlit water. Trenches are deep and dark, not suitable for coral reefs.

options.label: Kelp forests
options.feedback: Kelp requires sunlight and grows in shallow coastal waters, not in deep trenches.

items.exp_text: Fluid from subducting sediments returns to the surface at trenches, forming mud volcanoes and cold seeps. These support unique biomes based on chemotrophic microorganisms, which get energy from chemical reactions rather than light.

items.prompt: What is the depth range of trenches in the western Pacific, like the Mariana and Tonga-Kermadec?

options.label: 3 to 4 kilometers
options.feedback: That is the typical depth of trenches generally above the surrounding seafloor, but the western Pacific trenches are deeper, reaching 10-11 km.

options.label: 7 to 8 kilometers
options.feedback: That is the depth of the Peru-Chile trench in the eastern Pacific. Western Pacific trenches are deeper, up to 11 km.

options.label: 10 to 11 kilometers
options.feedback: Correct. The Marianas and Tonga-Kermadec trenches have bottoms up to 10-11 kilometers below sea level.

options.label: 12 to 13 kilometers
options.feedback: That is too deep. The deepest measured is about 10,994 meters, so 12-13 km is not supported.

items.exp_text: In the western Pacific, where older oceanic lithosphere subducts, trenches like the Marianas and Tonga-Kermadec have bottoms 10-11 kilometers below sea level. This is deeper than eastern Pacific trenches, which are about 7-8 km deep.

items.prompt: What happens when buoyant continental crust enters a trench?

options.label: Subduction halts and a collision zone forms
options.feedback: Correct. Buoyant continental crust does not sink easily, so subduction stops and the area becomes a continental collision zone.

options.label: The trench deepens rapidly
options.feedback: Continental crust is buoyant, so it does not deepen a trench. Instead, subduction stops.

options.label: A volcanic arc forms directly in the trench
options.feedback: Volcanic arcs form on the overriding plate, not from continental crust entering a trench. Subduction halts in this case.

options.label: The trench fills with sediments instantly
options.feedback: While sediments can fill trenches, the key result of continental crust entering is halting subduction, not instant filling.

items.exp_text: When buoyant continental crust enters a trench, subduction comes to a halt and the area becomes a zone of continental collision. This is different from oceanic lithosphere, which subducts into the mantle.
